scenario: Robots need to remember earlier events, choose current motion and determine how much force to exert. WholeBodyMem retains vanished object cues, while Ctrl-F separates force commands from reference motion. RoboARCade adds a reminder: execution still needs independent completion checks. The question is not whether a trajectory looks impressive, but whether observation, decision and execution form a reliable loop.

papers.title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
papers.authors: Mateo Clémente, George Z. Xue, Amin Abyaneh, Liheng Ma, Rui Heng Yang, Tongtong Cao, Zhanguang Zhang, Yingxue Zhang
papers.abstract: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on pretrained vision-language backbones; both tie policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. It remains unclear how much these generation-oriented choices affect control. In this work, we introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder. Following Fast-WAM, La-JEPA learns to predict future features jointly with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art performance in clean and randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes and on LIBERO-Plus with correct instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competing policies. It runs substantially faster than Fast-WAM at comparable performance and outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0 without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to pi0.5 and above non-embodied-pretrained baselines. Through a design study of the choices behind La-JEPA, we show that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction choices significantly impact the policy even when future prediction is skipped at inference. We correct the LIBERO-Plus instructions, as the officially released evaluator corrupts them for most variants, and re-evaluate several strong open baselines. Without a generative pretrained policy backbone, La-JEPA is better and faster than far larger policies, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.
papers.scoring_note: 具身方法或主要机器人评估
papers.summary: Learning to predict the future during robot training need not require generating it before every action. La-JEPA jointly learns actions and future visual features, but masks future features from the action pathway. At inference it removes future tokens, caches observation KV once per layer and repeatedly denoises only actions. With original-kernel CUDA graphs, the S model’s full policy-call speed still reached 2.6 times optimized Fast-WAM. This measures a policy call, not the complete robot control loop; future supervision primarily shapes observation representations during training.

papers.title: Open-HumanWAM: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models
papers.authors: Juncheng Ma, Jiaxin Li, Jiankai Tu, Bo Liang, Guodong Lv, Yufan Deng, Junzhe Tang, Liangzhu Yang, Chen Bian, Shukai Gong, Yintianrun Zhang, Zicong Cao, Baohao Zhu, Jianxin Bi, Tengfei Yan, Yinyuan Zhang, Kewei Zhang, Xinglong Chen, Kaiqi Chen, Duomin Wang, Xiaotian Tang, Liang Tan, Li Li, Yuan Xu, Haosen Yang, Yuqi Wang, Jingfei Xia, Songyan Huang, Zhiyang Dou, Zhen Dong, Enze Xie, Tat-Seng Chua, Daquan Zhou
papers.abstract: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanWAM, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanWAM-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world--action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human--robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world--action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanWAM-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.
papers.scoring_note: 具身方法或主要机器人评估
papers.summary: Human manipulation videos need consistent action semantics before they can teach robots. Open-HumanWAM aligns hand position, orientation and opening in camera coordinates, filtering invisible hands, unstable trajectories and long idle segments. Under an attention mask allowing action tokens to read the current frame but not future video frames, ten thousand hours of human pretraining followed by the same robot post-training raised randomized-scene success from 2.1% without that pretraining stage to 28.7%. Evaluation selects the best checkpoint separately for each setting; these are not all optimal results from a single model checkpoint.

papers.title: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation
papers.authors: Siyuan Hu, Abulikemu Abuduweili, Yue Meng, Shipeng Liu, Quentin Leboutet, Chen Chen, Matthias Müller, Vladlen Koltun
papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have the potential to automate a wide range of physical tasks. Progress toward generalist humanoid autonomy, however, remains constrained by a data bottleneck: mapping pixels and free-form language to low-level joint commands requires paired supervision, and no corpus of such data exists at sufficiently large scale. Some approaches rely on human teleoperation and wearable capture devices, which require at least an hour of human time to produce an hour of data. We present HALO, a humanoid autonomy system powered by a pipeline that synthesizes vision-language-motion data across a thousand procedurally generated homes. The corpus scales with compute rather than human labor. HALO acquires a repertoire of physical skills, including sitting on chairs, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes. It orchestrates these skills to solve composite, long-horizon tasks. Without ever seeing a real home during training, HALO transfers zero-shot to the physical world, achieving a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-halo/ for code and videos.
papers.scoring_note: 具身方法或主要机器人评估
papers.summary: In an unscanned room, finding a chair and sitting stably are different problems. HALO synthesizes vision–language–whole-body motion data in procedurally generated rooms. A high-level controller decomposes tasks, an RGB-based generator proposes motion, and a depth-and-proprioception tracker grounds execution. Single-skill physical evaluation in unseen environments achieved 91% success over 360 trials. This demonstrates transfer for the tested skill repertoire, not the same success rate on long-horizon tasks; motion priors, task-decomposition templates and low-level physical constraints remain important.

papers.title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Chenyuan Chen, Ran Ding, Lechen Zhang, Zewen He, Yoshihiko Nakamura
papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).
papers.scoring_note: 具身方法或主要机器人评估
papers.summary: After a robot turns away and returns, identical-looking seats may only be distinguishable through an earlier view. WholeBodyMem uses SAM3 to track task objects, removes camera motion and retains frames of events such as appearance, disappearance or movement. The action model reads those views and object features. Across 60 physical G1 trials, the complete system raised success from the base policy’s 36.7% to 88.3%. The gain includes object features and a decision module, not merely extra frames; cues the tracker never detects cannot automatically enter memory.

papers.title: Correct Robots Before They Make Mistakes: Proactive Human-in-the-Loop Intervention via Preference Learning
papers.authors: Xinkai Jiang, Jing Jiang, Hongyi Zhou, Pankhuri Vanjani, Ahmad Baki, Jakub Suliga, Ge Li, Zhuoyue Li, Gerhard Neumann, Rudolf Lioutikov
papers.abstract: This paper presents Proactive Human-in-the-Loop (PHIL), a framework for proactive policy correction and preference-based post-training. PHIL enables operators to preview policy-predicted future motion and intervene before anticipated undesirable actions. During takeover, PHIL continues querying the policy and displaying its predicted trajectories in the physical workspace through an extended reality (XR) interface. PHIL pairs rejected policy predictions with corrective action chunks subsequently executed from the same physical state over the same horizon, and preference-based post-training encourages the policy to favor these corrections. This paper evaluates PHIL on four real-world manipulation tasks using a diffusion policy and a pretrained vision-language-action policy. With five correction episodes per condition, PHIL increases mean success rates across the evaluated tasks and demonstration budgets from 44.0% to 70.3% for the diffusion policy and from 57.8% to 76.9% for X-VLA, compared with HG-DAgger. Separately, policies trained with proactive corrections show fewer unnecessary recovery behaviors in successful episodes. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/PHIL-page/.
papers.scoring_note: 具身方法或主要机器人评估
papers.summary: Waiting until a robot errs can fill correction data with unnecessary recovery actions. PHIL overlays predicted trajectories on the physical workspace through an extended-reality (XR) headset so operators can intervene proactively. During takeover the policy keeps proposing motion; rejected predictions pair with subsequent executed corrections from the same state and over the same horizon. Preference training is combined with imitation of original demonstrations. With five correction rollouts per condition, diffusion-policy mean success rose from HG-DAgger’s 44.0% to 70.3%. This combines preview, proactive collection and preference learning; it is not evidence that an interface alone guarantees safety.

papers.title: A³-VLA: Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Shengzhe Zhang, Qi Zhang, Dazhong Shen, Chao Wang, Shaopeng Zhai, Hui Xiong
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) enable robots to perform manipulation tasks by leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to process visual observations and language instructions. However, the action prediction objective itself lacks fine-grained task-specific perceptual supervision, making it prone to relying on task-irrelevant visual shortcuts, leading attention away from target objects and key interaction areas, thereby limiting its operational performance and generalization ability. To address this, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation ($A^3$-VLA), a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself. Specifically, $A^3$-VLA first generates heuristic candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, and refines them with a visual segmentation model offline. These regions serve as explicit perceptual guidance through two complementary objectives: an attention allocation loss that encourages sufficient focus on task-critical regions when language or robot state tokens query the visual input, and a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of candidate target regions with language instructions while separating them from task-irrelevant regions. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that $A^3$-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones, with an average success rate gain of 6.5% - 25.2% across benchmarks.
papers.scoring_note: 具身方法或主要机器人评估
papers.summary: A robot may understand which object to pick yet allocate attention elsewhere. A3-VLA identifies demonstration regions stable before interaction but changing afterward, then tracks candidate targets with SAM2. Training penalizes insufficient language-to-target and state-to-robot attention mass, while aligning target features with instructions. On RoboTwin, π0’s mean success improved by 9.8 percentage points. The regions provide soft supervision rather than exact ground truth; inference runs only the fine-tuned VLA, without an additional segmentation module.

papers.title: Ctrl-F: Force as an Interface for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Mengjie Zhao, Yuxin Chen, Yiyang Shao, Chuye Hong, Jiakang Chen, Koushil Sreenath, Masayoshi Tomizuka
papers.abstract: Humanoid motion tracking has scaled to general policies that reproduce diverse human motion, but the resulting behavior is in free-space: the tracker knows where the body should be, not how it should interact with the environment. Other work makes the object part of the objective, yet abstracts that interaction to contact or geometry, which leaves the demanding cases under-explored. We argue that force is a natural command channel between motion imitation and object interaction, one that specifies not just where to make contact but how hard. We present Ctrl-F, a hierarchical motion-force framework that augments motion tracking with an explicit force command, a 3-D force at each designated contact body such as a hand or a foot. The hierarchical framework comprises: (1) A unified motion-force controller tracks the reference motion while applying the commanded force to the world. (2) A high-level force planner that issues a force command online based on object state and proprioception observations. In simulation and on hardware, Ctrl-F completes loco-manipulation that demands large, sustained interaction force and adjusts its command online as the load changes, both out of reach of a force-blind tracker. On hardware, Ctrl-F demonstrates hand-based dragging, pushing, and lifting, as well as foot-based kicking, successfully manipulating boxes weighing up to 20kg in pushing and kicking tasks where the force-blind baseline fails, while adapting online to additional loads introduced mid-task.
papers.scoring_note: 具身方法或主要机器人评估
papers.summary: Dragging a heavy object requires more than reproducing motion: exerted force must change with load. Ctrl-F uses contact force as the interface between two levels. An object-free simulated tracker learns to resist opposing external forces while following motion; a higher-level planner adjusts force using discrepancies between actual and reference object motion. A G1 hardware demonstration dragged a locked-wheel cart carrying 14 kg of added load but failed at 20 kg. Object state currently depends on AprilTags, and unseen motions require retraining; one force interface does not imply immediate execution of arbitrary motion.

papers.title: Learning Object-Centric Motion Priors from Human for Robotic Dexterous Manipulation
papers.abstract: Manipulating diverse objects with multi-fingered dexterous hands is challenging due to the high dimensionality and complex dynamics. Human-Object Interaction (HOI) datasets provide rich knowledge about task information and embodied interactions. Instead of solely imitating the human demonstrations, our method learns to holistically predict future hand-object states by leveraging these datasets. The predicted future states of the object can serve as a general-purpose reward term for reinforcement learning, reducing reliance on task-specific reward engineering and enhancing generalization across tasks. We conduct extensive experiments on three manipulation tasks in simulation and the real world. Our approach outperforms existing SOTA methods in both success rate and generalizability on novel objects. Furthermore, we validate the cross-embodiment compatibility of our methods by successfully deploying the skills on different robot hands.
papers.scoring_note: 具身方法或主要机器人评估
papers.summary: Teaching a dexterous hand requires checking object motion, not just how human-like the fingers look. This method learns future hand–object trajectories from human interaction data, retargets hand motion to the robot, and uses PPO to reward both robot and object tracking. Experiments cover grasping, articulated-object manipulation and obstacle-aware grasping; ablations identify object tracking as important to learning efficiency. Object models, pose estimates and engineered contact rewards remain necessary. A different robotic hand requires new retargeting and policy training, not zero-training transfer of an identical policy.

papers.title: Where Is VLA Inference Time Spent? Bottlenecks and Optimization Interactions Across GPUs
papers.authors: Muhammad Danish Waseem, Ahmed Ali-Eldin Hassan
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera observations and language instructions to robot actions. However, their large backbones and repeated action generation can make inference take longer than the robot's real-time requirements for its next action. To reduce the load of VLA computations, researchers have proposed multiple optimization approaches, including quantization and pruning. These optimizations can be combined with other general optimizations such as better kernel compilation or using CUDA graphs instead of the eager mode. However, most of these optimization results are usually reported on a single GPU type, typically for a few VLA models, with no analysis of what the real bottlenecks are for a model on a particular hardware or how these optimizations would generalize beyond the reported results. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive measurement study of seven families of inference optimization methods, from CUDA graphs and compilation to token pruning and quantization, on seven state-of-the-art VLAs evaluated on four GPU families ranging from a datacenter H100 to an embedded Jetson Thor. We analyse how CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency jointly shape optimization gains, and how applying one method changes the benefit of another. From this analysis, we derive VLA-Triage, guidelines for stacking optimizations under latency budgets. The guidelines identify which stages can provide the required savings and which combinations need testing in the deployed execution mode.
papers.scoring_note: 具身方法或主要机器人评估
papers.summary: Compiling first and pruning tokens afterward does not let their separately measured speedups stack unchanged. VLA-Triage finds that once compilation shortens a stage, later optimizations have different time left to save. For CogACT on A10G, the saving from the same 75% pruning fell from 74.2 ms in eager execution to 33.5 ms after compilation. Quantization can replace kernels, while pruning changes matrix shapes, so combinations need measurement in the deployed execution mode. Timing starts after image preprocessing and ends at action output, not across the full robot control loop.

papers.title: RoboARCade: Benchmarking Agentic Robot Control
papers.authors: Satvik Sharma, Hengyuan Hu, Mihika Kamat, Dorsa Sadigh, Jeannette Bohg
papers.abstract: Improvements in multi-modal capabilities have enabled agents to act directly as robot policies, a setting we refer to as agentic robot control (ARC). We introduce RoboARCade, a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks across three embodiments designed to test in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning for precise control. The tasks build on existing open-source benchmarks, which we make harder by widening the range of initial conditions. RoboARCade is easy to use and extend: all tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, each task is a self-contained data pack, and agents connect through interchangeable interfaces, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently. The benchmark separates leading agents: GPT-6 Astra achieves 49.8% compared with 43.6% for Claude Fable 5.1, leaving substantial room for improvement. Comparing two interfaces, we find that a richer visual interface adds only 1.5 to 6.8 points at 1.7 to 2.3 times the cost. Failures stem mostly from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely, rarely from misunderstanding the scene, and agents incorrectly claim success on 24% to 39% of attempted subtasks. Agents can also improve without human input: one successful demonstration in context raises Astra's score from 53.5% to 73.0% on a five-task subset, and a prompt the agent writes and revises itself reaches 72.0%. Code, videos and full traces are available at roboarcade.org.
papers.scoring_note: 具身方法或主要机器人评估
papers.summary: A robot agent declaring completion does not establish task success. RoboARCade separates the agent from privileged simulator state and grading rules, exposing visual, depth or 3D interaction interfaces while an external grader evaluates subtasks. On a subset of tasks with existing successful examples, reading one same-task demonstration raised mean rubric score from 53.5% to 73.0%; this is not full-task success rate. Demonstrations reduce timeouts on bad approaches, but precise placement and false completion claims persist. Explaining a procedure, completing it and recognizing completion need separate evaluation.
